overview: Purpose: This page is the canonical deployment reference for Redwood Private (VPC and on‑prem). It consolidates architecture patterns, detailed deployment steps, packaging guidance for air‑gapped/on‑prem installations, Day‑2 operational tasks, upgrade and rollback procedures, and the customer requirements checklist used by Solutions Engineering. Scope: Hosted private control plane (customer‑managed), on‑prem packaging (tarballs/containers), VPC deployment in customer cloud accounts, and post‑deployment operations. Not in scope: internal hosted API (public cloud) runbook specifics and product roadmap discussion.
audience_and_prerequisites: Audience: Solutions Engineers, Customer SREs/Platform teams, Redwood Private delivery engineers. Prerequisites: Customer point of contact and technical owners, cloud account with admin permissions (if VPC), network topology diagram, approved IP ranges and firewall rules, KMS/HSM details for envelope encryption, registry access for images or S3/HTTPS for air‑gap payloads. Minimum access (VPC): IAM role with ability to create VPC/subnets/SGs/EC2/EKS/ALB, S3 access for artifacts. On‑prem prerequisites: Linux hosts (RHEL/CentOS/Ubuntu LTS), access to hypervisor/container runtime (Docker or containerd), at least one dedicated GPU host (if using GPU inference), available NFS/SMB or object store for model artifacts, and an offline transfer medium if air‑gapped.
reference_architectures:
We maintain three validated reference patterns; choose based on scale, compliance, and operational model:

- Pattern A: Small single‑AZ VPC (pilot / PoC)
  - Use when: <10 QPS, non‑critical latency tolerances, rapid onboarding.
  - Components: 1 private subnet for control plane agents, 1 private subnet for inference nodes (EC2/GPU), NAT gateway, internal ALB for routing, Bastion host in public subnet for support (or SSM).
  - Sizing: 1-2 GPU instances (g4dn.xlarge / g5.xlarge) + m5.large control plane.

- Pattern B: Production multi‑AZ VPC (recommended for most customers)
  - Use when: production traffic, availability SLOs >= 99.9%.
  - Components: Dedicated control plane VPC (or customer-managed private endpoint to Redwood control plane), 3 AZs, per‑AZ inference node pools (GPU compute ASGs / node groups), internal NLB/ALB with cross‑AZ targets, private endpoints to object store (S3 VPC endpoint), KMS integration via endpoint or proxy, EKS or managed Kubernetes recommended.
  - Sizing guidance: Start with 3x p4d‑like or g5.12xlarge equivalents for medium workloads; scale by throughput.

- Pattern C: Air‑gapped on‑prem (regulated / high‑security)
  - Use when: no outbound network or strict data residency.
  - Components: On‑prem orchestration (Kubernetes), local registry, HSM/KMS appliance, dedicated model artifact store, optional hardware load balancer, ingress via customer perimeter DMZ.
  - Packaging: Signed tarball with container images, checksum file, installation script, and verification report.
vpc_deployment_guide:
This section is a prescriptive step‑by‑step guide for deploying Redwood Private into a customer VPC.

Preflight checks (must be completed before provisioning):
1) Validate account-level permissions: ability to create VPC, subnets, route tables, security groups, EC2/EKS, IAM roles, S3 endpoints.
2) Obtain network info: CIDR block (e.g., 10.10.0.0/16), AZ preference, approved public egress IP ranges, and firewall allowlist for Redwood control plane endpoints.
3) KMS/HSM: Provide CMK ARN or HSM connection details for envelope encryption.
4) Secrets: Access to container registry credentials or S3 location for images.

Step 1 — Network setup:
- Create VPC and subnets: private-subnet-1/2/3 in each AZ for inference; management subnet for control plane agents.
- Route tables: Ensure private subnets route to NAT gateway for outbound updates (unless strictly blocked).
- VPC endpoints: Add interface endpoints for KMS and SSM if required; gateway endpoint for S3.
- Security groups:
  - ControlPlane-SG: allow inbound from Redwood Control Plane IPs on TLS (443) if using private control plane tunnel; allow SSH (22) from bastion CIDR if enabled; allow internal ports for health/probes (e.g., 8080/9000).
  - Inference-SG: allow inbound from internal ALB/NLB on inference ports (default 8080), allow health checks, egress to object store and telemetry endpoints.

Step 2 — Compute & orchestration:
- Provision EKS cluster (recommended) or ECS/VMs. Recommended EKS add‑ons: aws-node, kube‑proxy, metrics‑server, VPC CNI.
- Node groups: label nodes by capability (gpu=true, nvlink=true). Use GPU AMIs with required drivers and CUDA/toolkits.
- Storage: configure PVs for models (NFS, EBS, or S3 via CSI).

Step 3 — Deploy control plane agents and runtime:
- Apply CRDs/Helm charts (we provide signed Helm chart vX.Y.Z). Example: helm install redwood-control ./charts/control-plane --set image.registry=..., --set ingress.type=internal.
- Configure TLS: use ACM or customer TLS cert on ALB; ensure internal DNS entries resolve to ALB.
- Connect to Redwood control plane: register tenant ID and provide connector key via Kubernetes secret.

Step 4 — Networking and security validation:
- Verify S3 access via VPC endpoint and that egress is blocked except to allowed control plane IPs.
- Test KMS encryption by performing an artifact upload and verifying server‑side encryption logs.

Step 5 — Smoke tests:
- Push a small model (tokenizer + model <1GB) and run inference against health endpoint.
- Validate metrics ingestion to Prometheus/Grafana and logging to customer ELK/CloudWatch.

Operational notes and SLOs:
- Latency SLO target: p50 < 60ms for small requests (subject to model/hardware).
- Availability SLO: 99.9% for production multi‑AZ deployments.
- Monitoring: export token latency, request rate, model cache hit ratio, GPU utilization, host memory pressure, and KV cache size.

Common troubleshooting commands (Kubernetes):
- kubectl get pods -n redwood
- kubectl logs deploy/redwood-runtime -n redwood --tail=200
- kubectl exec -n redwood deploy/redwood-runtime -- curl -f http://localhost:8080/healthz
onprem_packaging:
On‑prem packaging options and air‑gap distribution strategy. Use when customer cannot pull images from public registries.

Deliverables: signed_release.tar.gz containing:
- container_images.tar (OCI image tarball produced by 'skopeo sync' or 'docker save')
- helm_charts.tgz (signed)
- install.sh (idempotent installer with preflight checks)
- checksums.sha256 and signed_checksums.sha256.sig (GPG)
- manifest.json (list of images, versions, checksums)

Packaging steps (Redwood delivery engineer):
1) Generate release: build images and tag to release version (e.g., rwinference-private-2026.04.01).
2) Export images: docker save / skopeo copy to local tarball.
3) Sign artifacts: generate SHA256 checksums and sign with Redwood release GPG key.
4) Produce install bundle: run packaging script to assemble tar.gz and manifest.
5) Test installation in an isolated lab environment (air‑gap testbed) and generate verification report.

Customer installation steps (high level):
1) Transfer bundle to internal jump host.
2) Verify GPG signatures and checksums.
3) Run install.sh with provided arguments (namespace, storage path, KMS config).
4) Validate health checks and run smoke inference.

Air‑gap operational notes:
- Image updates: incremental delta bundles recommended to reduce transfer size.
- Security: signed bundles and verification required for compliance.
- Artifact retention: recommend keeping last 3 release bundles for rollback support.
day2_ops:
Day‑2 procedures and runbooks for common operational tasks. This section is actionable and should be used for handoffs to customer SREs.

1) Scaling compute
- Horizontal scaling: increase node group desired count or add additional GPU node pools. For EKS: kubectl scale --replicas=N deployment/redwood-inference-pool -n redwood.
- Vertical scaling: replace node group instance types (drain nodes and roll new ones). Use graceful pod eviction and PodDisruptionBudgets.

2) Model lifecycle operations
- Deploy model: upload artifact to model store (S3/NFS), create Model CR (or call admin API) to register model version, wait for caching.
- Remove model: deprecate model version in admin API, run asynchronous cleanup for local caches.

3) Backup & restore
- Back up metadata DB daily (Postgres snapshot) and model store incremental sync nightly.
- Restore test: quarterly restore drill to validate backups. Document RTO/RPO.

4) Monitoring & alerts (examples):
- Critical alerts: control plane disconnected >5m, GPU memory pressure >90% for 5m, inference error rate >5% for 10m.
- Warning alerts: model cache hit ratio <60% for 30m, host disk usage >80%.

5) Log management
- Retention: default 30 days for logs, 90 days for aggregated metrics (customer choice).
- Rotation: use logrotate system or sidecar to push to customer logging endpoint.

6) Routine maintenance
- Security patching: schedule monthly patch window for control plane agents and node OS; provide hotfix procedure for critical vulnerabilities.
- Model validation: run nightly evals on a small in‑house prompt set to detect regressions.

7) Common incident runbooks (short summaries):
- High inference latency: check GPU saturation, queue depth, KV cache hit rate. Scale pools or throttle requests.
- Control plane disconnect: confirm network egress rules, validate control plane cert TTL, restart control plane agent.
- Model load failures: verify artifact checksum, S3 endpoint connectivity, and container image availability.

Each runbook references a full incident playbook (see related_pages).
upgrade_and_rollback:
Guided upgrade and rollback playbook. All upgrades MUST follow the canary + staged rollout procedure unless approved otherwise.

Pre-upgrade (must complete):
- Backup metadata DB and snapshot model store.
- Verify smoke test baseline metrics and document current deployment version.
- Ensure preflight checks pass: available node capacity, disk space, network connectivity.

Upgrade steps (canary pattern):
1) Publish new Helm chart and image to registry (or prepare air‑gap bundle).
2) Canary deploy to 1 AZ / 5% of traffic: helm upgrade --install redwood-runtime --namespace redwood --set rollout.canary=true --set rollout.weight=5
3) Run canary validation for 30–60 minutes: compare latency, error rate, cache hit ratio, memory use to baseline. Use automated canary analysis (preferred).
4) Gradually increase traffic (5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with validation gates at each stage.
5) After 100% traffic and 24 hours of stability, mark release as promoted and create release note.

Rollback procedure (if any validation gate fails):
1) Immediately stop traffic to new version (set rollout.weight back to 0 or scale down canary pods).
2) Revert Helm release to previous chart/image: helm rollback redwood-runtime <revision>.
3) If DB schema migration occurred and is irreversible, follow the documented migration rollback steps (precreated downgrade migration scripts required).
4) Postmortem: capture heap/profile traces, collect logs, and open incident with root cause analysis.

Notes on DB migrations:
- Use backward‑compatible migrations where possible. If a breaking migration is required, schedule a maintenance window and run a preflight in a staging environment. Maintain explicit migration rollback scripts in the release bundle.
customer_requirements_library:
This section contains the standard questionnaire and minimal technical requirements we collect during pre‑sales and staging. Use as a template when onboarding new private customers.

Required customer inputs (table style represented in text):
- Network and Access:
  - VPC CIDR(s): e.g., 10.10.0.0/16
  - Allowed outbound IPs / firewall allowlist: list of Redwood control plane IPs
  - Public/Private subnet mapping for control plane and inference hosts
  - DNS: internal domain and wildcard DNS for ALB

- Identity & Security:
  - IAM role (arn) for provisioning or admin account credentials
  - KMS: CMK ARN or HSM connection details
  - Certificate management: ACM ARN or TLS cert bundle (pem key cert)
  - RBAC requirements and SSO/OIDC provider details

- Storage & Artifacts:
  - Model store: S3 bucket (or NFS endpoint) details, access method, encryption at rest requirements
  - Artifact transfer method (registry access or air‑gap bundle)

- Compute & Hardware:
  - Expected peak QPS and latency targets
  - GPU instance preferences / on‑prem GPU spec (GPU model, memory, NVLink)
  - Node count and AZs to use

- Compliance & Operational:
  - Data residency / retention policy
  - Audit logging requirements and log shipping destination
  - Backup windows and RTO/RPO expectations

- Contacts & Escalation:
  - Primary technical contact (name, email, pager)
  - Security contact and emergency escalation path

We keep a canonical CSV template that Solutions Engineering uses; attach the filled template to the customer ticket before kickoff.
operational_checklist:
Pre‑deployment checklist (for SE & delivery):
- [ ] Customer questionnaire completed and signed
- [ ] Account permissions verified and IAM role provisioned
- [ ] KMS/HSM details confirmed and test keys provided
- [ ] Network allowlist and VPC subnets reserved
- [ ] Storage (S3/NFS) access verified
- [ ] Installer bundle validated (on‑prem) or Helm chart access confirmed (VPC)
- [ ] Monitoring destination (Prometheus/Grafana or Cloud) configured
- [ ] Backup schedule and snapshot policy documented

Post‑deployment handoff checklist:
- [ ] Smoke tests passed and documented
- [ ] SLO baseline metrics collected for 72h
- [ ] Runbooks handed off to customer SRE with access to runbook repo
- [ ] Scheduled first monthly patch window
- [ ] Escalation contacts confirmed and loaded into oncall roster
